title: Great is peace (Leviticus Rabbah 9:9)
hookLine: even God changed words for peace, and the blessings all end with peace
tomorrow: how did Aaron get two people who wouldn't talk to make up?

lines: DID SHE SAY ANYTHING ABOUT ME?
cards: A friend asks: did she say anything about me? And she did. Something sharp, said on a bad day.
Do you repeat it word for word? Honesty seems to say yes. Kindness seems to say no.
And your friend is still waiting, watching your face for the answer before you've even typed it. Leviticus Rabbah answers yesterday's question with a surprise: once, God edited a quote.

teach.b: When Sarah hears she'll have a child, she laughs, and in the King James words she says, "my lord being old also." When God repeats it to Abraham, the line becomes: "Shall I of a surety bear a child, which am old?"

Abraham's age has quietly dropped out. Nobody in the story points it out; the midrash is the one that notices. The midrash says: great is peace, for even the Holy One changed words for the sake of peace.
And it adds that the blessings end in peace; the priestly blessing closes, "and give thee peace." So may you shade the truth for peace? The tradition argues about it, and both sides get to speak.
The Talmud asks: what do you sing while dancing before a bride?
Beit Shammai says: describe the bride as she is.
Beit Hillel says: a beautiful and graceful bride. Shammai pushes back. What if she's lame or blind?
The Torah says, "Keep thee far from a false matter." Hillel answers with a question. If someone made a poor purchase in the market, do you praise it to them or run it down?
Praise it. You could put Shammai's case like this: if every bride is beautiful, the word stops meaning anything.
And Hillel's like this: at a wedding, the words aren't a report, they're a gift. Notice what God didn't do with Sarah. No invented praise.
Just one hurtful phrase, left out.

how: Jewish prayers often close on peace: the priestly blessing ends 'and give thee peace', and the Amidah's last blessing asks for peace. The Talmud records Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai disagreeing over how to praise a bride (Ketubot 16b–17a).

o: a calm, quiet mind is the goal of every prayer
peace matters so much that even God bent words for it
peace treaties have to be signed before every war

games.q: truth and peace — tap the pairs.
p: describe the bride as she is

s: when God tells Abraham about Sarah's laugh, it's word for word
her line about Abraham being old drops out. the midrash: even God changed words for peace.
Beit Shammai's view rests on a verse from the Torah
'keep thee far from a false matter' (Exodus 23:7).
in the midrash, peace means saying whatever makes people feel good
God didn't add praise; one hurtful phrase was left out.

games.q: you lean toward Beit Hillel. a friend leans toward Beit Shammai. what's the strongest case for Shammai's side?
o: if every bride is called beautiful, the word stops meaning anything.
Shammai simply didn't care much about people's feelings at weddings.
Shammai thought weddings should be serious, with no dancing at all.
games.why: Shammai stands on the Torah's 'keep thee far from a false matter': his care is for words people can trust.

practice: Think of two people, or you and one person, where a small word could ease things. Write one sentence you could send: true, kind, and leaving out the part that only wounds. Send it if the time is right, or keep it ready until it is.

wordCard.voice: Great is peace: Leviticus Rabbah's line about the day God left Abraham's age out of Sarah's words. Even God changed a quote for the sake of peace.

orig.note: Hebrew: peace, wholeness. the word the priestly blessing ends on.

carryVoice: Carry this: great is peace. God didn't invent praise; one wounding phrase was simply left out.
